decks.title: Bordeaux 1855: the Médoc and Graves reds
decks.description: The 61 classed red growths of 1855 on the map: commune and rank for each.

cards.q: Find Château Lafite Rothschild. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Pauillac; First Growth. Listed first among the first growths in 1855, Lafite sits on the northern edge of Pauillac, its vines running down to the Jalle du Breuil stream that separates it from Cos d'Estournel in Saint-Estèphe.

cards.q: Find Château Latour. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Pauillac; First Growth. Latour takes its name from a fourteenth-century fort that guarded the estuary; the domed tower in the vines is a later dovecote.

cards.q: Find Château Margaux. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Margaux; First Growth. The only first growth in the Margaux appellation, and the only one whose château is a true neoclassical palace: Louis Combes built it between 1810 and 1816, columns and all.

cards.q: Where is Château Haut-Brion, and what is its 1855 rank?
cards.a: Pessac (Pessac-Léognan AOC, Graves). First Growth (Premier Cru Classé) in 1855, the only red outside the Médoc in the classification; also Cru Classé de Graves (1959).

cards.q: Find Château Mouton Rothschild. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Pauillac; First Growth (promoted 1973). The only estate ever promoted in the 1855 classification.

cards.q: Find Château Rauzan-Ségla. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Margaux; Second Growth. Pierre de Rauzan created this estate in 1661, and it was split in the eighteenth century into Rauzan-Ségla and Rauzan-Gassies.

cards.q: Find Château Rauzan-Gassies. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Margaux; Second Growth. The other half of Pierre de Rauzan's seventeenth-century estate, owned by the Quié family since 1946.

cards.q: Find Château Léoville Las Cases. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Saint-Julien; Second Growth. The largest share of the old Léoville estate, which was divided after the Revolution into Las Cases, Poyferré and Barton.

cards.q: Find Château Léoville Poyferré. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Saint-Julien; Second Growth. Named after Baron Jean-Marie de Poyferré, who inherited this third of the Léoville estate in the early nineteenth century.

cards.q: Find Château Léoville Barton. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Saint-Julien; Second Growth. Hugh Barton, of an Irish family of Bordeaux merchants, bought a third of the Léoville vineyard in 1826, five years after buying Langoa.

cards.q: Find Château Durfort-Vivens. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Margaux; Second Growth. Named after the Durfort de Duras family, who owned it from the fourteenth century.

cards.q: Find Château Gruaud Larose. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Saint-Julien; Second Growth. Founded in the 1720s by the abbé Gruaud and later passed to his heir, Monsieur de La Rose, it is one of the largest estates in Saint-Julien, set inland on a broad gravel plateau.

cards.q: Find Château Lascombes. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Margaux; Second Growth. Named after Antoine de Lascombes, a seventeenth-century owner.

cards.q: Find Château Brane-Cantenac. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Margaux; Second Growth. Baron Hector de Brane, nicknamed the 'Napoleon of the vines', sold Brane-Mouton (now Mouton Rothschild) in 1830 to concentrate on his estate in Cantenac.

cards.q: Find Château Pichon Baron. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Pauillac; Second Growth. In 1850 the Pichon-Longueville estate was divided between Baron Raoul de Pichon-Longueville and his sisters; the baron kept this half and built the turreted fairytale château in 1851.

cards.q: Find Château Pichon Longueville Comtesse de Lalande. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Pauillac; Second Growth. The sisters' share of the 1850 Pichon division, named after Virginie, Comtesse de Lalande.

cards.q: Find Château Ducru-Beaucaillou. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Saint-Julien; Second Growth. The name means Ducru (a nineteenth-century owner) plus 'beaux cailloux', beautiful stones, for the large gravel that covers its riverside vineyard.

cards.q: Find Château Cos d'Estournel. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Saint-Estèphe; Second Growth. Louis-Gaspard d'Estournel, who traded horses and wine with India, built the extraordinary chai with pagoda towers and a carved door from Zanzibar in the 1830s.

cards.q: Find Château Montrose. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Saint-Estèphe; Second Growth. Montrose did not exist as a vineyard until the early nineteenth century, when Étienne Théodore Dumoulin cleared a heath of pink heather on a gravel mound above the estuary.

cards.q: Find Château Kirwan. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Margaux; Third Growth. Named after Mark Kirwan, an Irishman from Galway who married into the estate in the eighteenth century.

cards.q: Find Château d'Issan. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Margaux; Third Growth. A moated seventeenth-century château built on the foundations of the medieval Château de la Mothe-Cantenac, beside the estuary meadows.

cards.q: Find Château Lagrange. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Saint-Julien; Third Growth. The largest estate in Saint-Julien, inland on two gravel hills behind Gruaud Larose, with an Italianate tower.

cards.q: Find Château Langoa Barton. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Saint-Julien; Third Growth. Bought by Hugh Barton in 1821, Langoa is the oldest classed growth to have remained with the same family, now the seventh and eighth Barton generations.

cards.q: Find Château Giscours. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Margaux; Third Growth. A large estate in Labarde with a grand Second Empire château and a park landscaped by Eugène Bühler.

cards.q: Find Château Malescot Saint-Exupéry. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Margaux; Third Growth. Simon Malescot, counsellor to King Louis XIV, bought the estate in 1697; Count Jean-Baptiste de Saint-Exupéry, an ancestor of the author of The Little Prince, owned it in the nineteenth century.

cards.q: Find Château Boyd-Cantenac. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Margaux; Third Growth. Named after Jacques Boyd, of an Irish family, who bought vines in Cantenac in the 1750s.

cards.q: Find Château Cantenac Brown. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Margaux; Third Growth. John Lewis Brown, of a Scottish family and father of the animal painter of the same name, built the château in the 1830s in an English Tudor style that looks nothing like any other building in the Médoc.

cards.q: Find Château Palmer. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Margaux; Third Growth. Major-General Charles Palmer, a British officer who fought under Wellington, bought the estate in 1814 and ruined himself on it; the Pereire banking brothers took it over in 1853.

cards.q: Find Château La Lagune. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Haut-Médoc AOC (commune of Ludon); Third Growth. The first classed growth heading north from Bordeaux, in Ludon on sandy gravel close to the estuary.

cards.q: Find Château Desmirail. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Margaux; Third Growth. Named after Jean Desmirail, who married into the Rauzan family in the eighteenth century.

cards.q: Find Château Calon-Ségur. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Saint-Estèphe; Third Growth. The most northerly classed growth, once owned by the Marquis de Ségur, who also owned Lafite and Latour but said his heart was at Calon: hence the heart on the label, a favourite Valentine's Day wine.

cards.q: Find Château Ferrière. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Margaux; Third Growth. One of the smallest classed growths, at under 25 ha, named after Gabriel Ferrière, a royal shipbroker.

cards.q: Find Château Marquis d'Alesme. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Margaux; Third Growth. Formerly Marquis d'Alesme Becker, this small estate in Margaux village was bought by the Perrodo family (also owners of Labégorce) in 2006.

cards.q: Find Château Saint-Pierre. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Saint-Julien; Fourth Growth. A small Saint-Julien estate bought in 1982 by Henri Martin, mayor of Saint-Julien and creator of Château Gloria, and now run by his descendants, the Triaud family.

cards.q: Find Château Talbot. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Saint-Julien; Fourth Growth. Named after John Talbot, Earl of Shrewsbury, the English commander killed at Castillon in 1453, though there is no proof he ever owned it.

cards.q: Find Château Branaire-Ducru. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Saint-Julien; Fourth Growth. Facing Beychevelle across the road, Branaire takes its name from Jean-Baptiste Braneyre, who bought it in 1680, and from the Ducru family of the nineteenth century.

cards.q: Find Château Duhart-Milon. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Pauillac; Fourth Growth. Bought by the Rothschilds of Lafite in 1962, Duhart-Milon's vines lie on the slopes of the Carruades plateau west of Lafite, next to the hamlet of Milon.

cards.q: Find Château Pouget. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Margaux; Fourth Growth. One of the smallest classed growths, about 10 ha in Cantenac, owned by the Guillemet family and made alongside Boyd-Cantenac.

cards.q: Find Château La Tour Carnet. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Haut-Médoc AOC (commune of Saint-Laurent-Médoc); Fourth Growth. A genuine medieval castle with a moat and a thirteenth-century keep, in Saint-Laurent-Médoc.

cards.q: Find Château Lafon-Rochet. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Saint-Estèphe; Fourth Growth. Instantly recognisable by its yellow château and label, painted that colour by the Tesseron family, who owned it from 1960 until 2021, when Jacky Lorenzetti (owner of Pédesclaux) bought it.

cards.q: Find Château Beychevelle. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Saint-Julien; Fourth Growth. Its name is said to derive from baisse-voile, lower the sail: ships on the Gironde dipped their sails to salute the Duc d'Épernon, admiral of France, who owned the estate in the seventeenth century.

cards.q: Find Château Prieuré-Lichine. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Margaux; Fourth Growth. Once the priory of the Benedictine monks of Cantenac, it was bought in 1951 by Alexis Lichine, the Russian-born wine writer and merchant, who added his name and opened it to visitors when such hospitality was unheard of in the Médoc.

cards.q: Find Château Marquis de Terme. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Margaux; Fourth Growth. Named after the Marquis de Terme, who acquired it by marriage in 1762.

cards.q: Find Château Pontet-Canet. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Pauillac; Fifth Growth. Owned by the Tesseron family since 1975, Pontet-Canet became the most talked-about fifth growth of the 2000s.

cards.q: Find Château Batailley. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Pauillac; Fifth Growth. Its name recalls a battle of the Hundred Years War said to have been fought on the site.

cards.q: Find Château Haut-Batailley. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Pauillac; Fifth Growth. Split off from Batailley in 1942 when the Borie family divided its holdings, Haut-Batailley was run by the Bories of Ducru-Beaucaillou until the Cazes family of Lynch-Bages bought it in 2017.

cards.q: Find Château Grand-Puy-Lacoste. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Pauillac; Fifth Growth. 'Puy' means hill: the estate sits on a high gravel mound on the Bages plateau.

cards.q: Find Château Grand-Puy Ducasse. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Pauillac; Fifth Growth. Unusually, its château stands on the waterfront quay of Pauillac town, while its vines are scattered across three parts of the appellation.

cards.q: Find Château Lynch-Bages. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Pauillac; Fifth Growth. Named after Thomas Lynch, of an Irish family, whose son Jean-Baptiste became mayor of Bordeaux.

cards.q: Find Château Lynch-Moussas. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Pauillac; Fifth Growth. The westernmost classed growth of Pauillac, on gravel at the edge of the forest.

cards.q: Find Château Dauzac. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Margaux; Fifth Growth. In Labarde, close to the estuary, Dauzac has a famous place in wine science.

cards.q: Find Château d'Armailhac. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Pauillac; Fifth Growth. Baron Philippe de Rothschild bought this neighbour of Mouton in 1933 and renamed it several times (Mouton Baron Philippe, then Mouton Baronne Philippe) before reverting in 1989 to the name of the eighteenth-century d'Armailhacq family.

cards.q: Find Château du Tertre. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Margaux; Fifth Growth. 'Tertre' means a small hill, and this estate in Arsac sits on one of the highest gravel ridges in the Margaux appellation.

cards.q: Find Château Haut-Bages Libéral. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Pauillac; Fifth Growth. Named after the Libéral family, eighteenth-century merchants.

cards.q: Find Château Pédesclaux. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Pauillac; Fifth Growth. Founded by Pierre Urbain Pédesclaux, a Bordeaux wine broker of the early nineteenth century, when brokers (courtiers) were the men who drew up the 1855 ranking.

cards.q: Find Château Belgrave. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Haut-Médoc AOC (commune of Saint-Laurent-Médoc); Fifth Growth. An inland estate in Saint-Laurent-Médoc, just behind Lagrange and the Saint-Julien border.

cards.q: Find Château de Camensac. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Haut-Médoc AOC (commune of Saint-Laurent-Médoc); Fifth Growth. An eighteenth-century chartreuse in Saint-Laurent-Médoc.

cards.q: Find Château Cos Labory. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Saint-Estèphe; Fifth Growth. A small estate next door to Cos d'Estournel, owned by the Audoy family.

cards.q: Find Château Clerc Milon. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Pauillac; Fifth Growth. Bought by Baron Philippe de Rothschild in 1970, its vines lie next to Lafite and Mouton close to the estuary, around the hamlet of Milon.

cards.q: Find Château Croizet-Bages. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Pauillac; Fifth Growth. On the Bages plateau next to Lynch-Bages, owned by the Quié family (also of Rauzan-Gassies) since 1942.

cards.q: Find Château Cantemerle. Appellation and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Haut-Médoc AOC (commune of Macau); Fifth Growth (added to the list in September 1855). Missing from the original list of April 1855, Cantemerle was added a few months later at the bottom of the fifth growths after its owner, the widow Villeneuve-Durfort, produced records proving its prices.

cards.q: How many red wines are in the 1855 classification, and which change was made in 1973?
cards.a: 61 châteaux (60 Médoc plus Haut-Brion). In 1973 Mouton Rothschild was promoted from second to first growth; the only other change was the addition of Cantemerle to the fifth growths soon after the list was drawn up.
cards.hint: Five tiers: 5 first, 14 second, 14 third, 10 fourth, 18 fifth growths

cards.q: Name the five first growths of the Médoc classification today.
cards.a: Lafite Rothschild, Latour, Mouton Rothschild (all Pauillac), Margaux (Margaux) and Haut-Brion (Pessac-Léognan).

cards.q: Which commune has the most classed growths in 1855, and how many?
cards.a: Margaux, with 21 of the 61 classed growths (Cantenac, Labarde, Arsac and Soussans are included in the AOC).

cards.q: On what basis did the Bordeaux brokers rank the wines in 1855?
cards.a: On trading prices over many years, for the Exposition Universelle in Paris, at the request of Napoleon III; not on a tasting or terroir survey.

decks.title: Bordeaux 1855: Sauternes and Barsac
decks.description: The 1855 sweet-wine classification: Yquem, the premiers and deuxièmes crus.

cards.q: Find Château d'Yquem. Commune and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Sauternes; Premier Cru Supérieur (Superior First Growth), the only one in the 1855 Sauternes-Barsac classification. The only wine given the rank of Premier Cru Supérieur in 1855, a title no red wine received.
cards.hint: Sauternes commune group: Sauternes, Bommes, Fargues, Preignac

cards.q: Find Château La Tour Blanche. Commune and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Sauternes; Premier Cru (First Growth) in the 1855 Sauternes-Barsac classification. Ranked first of the Premiers Crus after Yquem in 1855.
cards.hint: Sauternes commune group: Sauternes, Bommes, Fargues, Preignac

cards.q: Find Château Lafaurie-Peyraguey. Commune and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Sauternes; Premier Cru (First Growth) in the 1855 Sauternes-Barsac classification. A thirteenth-century fortified manor in Bommes with crenellated walls.
cards.hint: Sauternes commune group: Sauternes, Bommes, Fargues, Preignac

cards.q: Find Clos Haut-Peyraguey. Commune and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Sauternes; Premier Cru (First Growth) in the 1855 Sauternes-Barsac classification. Created when the Peyraguey estate was divided in 1879, this small vineyard on the summit of the Bommes hill was owned by the Pauly family for a century before Bernard Magrez bought it in 2012.
cards.hint: Sauternes commune group: Sauternes, Bommes, Fargues, Preignac

cards.q: Find Château de Rayne Vigneau. Commune and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Sauternes; Premier Cru (First Growth) in the 1855 Sauternes-Barsac classification. On a hill in Bommes famous for its soil studded with semi-precious stones, agate, onyx and quartz brought by the Garonne, which a nineteenth-century owner had catalogued.
cards.hint: Sauternes commune group: Sauternes, Bommes, Fargues, Preignac

cards.q: Find Château Suduiraut. Commune and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Sauternes; Premier Cru (First Growth) in the 1855 Sauternes-Barsac classification. A grand seventeenth-century château in Preignac with gardens attributed to André Le Nôtre's school, bordering Yquem's vines.
cards.hint: Sauternes commune group: Sauternes, Bommes, Fargues, Preignac

cards.q: Find Château Coutet. Commune and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Barsac; Premier Cru (First Growth) in the 1855 Sauternes-Barsac classification. The largest of the Barsac first growths, with a thirteenth-century tower that once served as an English fort.
cards.hint: Barsac sits north of the Ciron on limestone

cards.q: Find Château Climens. Commune and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Barsac; Premier Cru (First Growth) in the 1855 Sauternes-Barsac classification. Often called the Lord of Barsac, Climens farms about 30 ha in one block on the highest point of the Barsac limestone plateau, planted entirely with Sémillon.
cards.hint: Barsac sits north of the Ciron on limestone

cards.q: Find Château Guiraud. Commune and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Sauternes; Premier Cru (First Growth) in the 1855 Sauternes-Barsac classification. One of the largest estates of Sauternes, on gravel next to Yquem.
cards.hint: Sauternes commune group: Sauternes, Bommes, Fargues, Preignac

cards.q: Find Château Rieussec. Commune and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Sauternes; Premier Cru (First Growth) in the 1855 Sauternes-Barsac classification. In Fargues, on high gravel next to Yquem.
cards.hint: Sauternes commune group: Sauternes, Bommes, Fargues, Preignac

cards.q: Find Château Rabaud-Promis. Commune and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Sauternes; Premier Cru (First Growth) in the 1855 Sauternes-Barsac classification. The old Rabaud estate in Bommes was ranked as one in 1855, divided in 1903 into Rabaud-Promis and Sigalas-Rabaud, reunited in 1929 and divided again in 1952.
cards.hint: Sauternes commune group: Sauternes, Bommes, Fargues, Preignac

cards.q: Find Château Sigalas Rabaud. Commune and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Sauternes; Premier Cru (First Growth) in the 1855 Sauternes-Barsac classification. The smaller half of the old Rabaud estate, on a gravel slope in Bommes facing north-west.
cards.hint: Sauternes commune group: Sauternes, Bommes, Fargues, Preignac

cards.q: Find Château de Myrat. Commune and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Barsac; Deuxième Cru (Second Growth) in the 1855 Sauternes-Barsac classification. The de Pontac family, owners since the nineteenth century, pulled up the vines in 1976 when Sauternes could not be sold.
cards.hint: Barsac sits north of the Ciron on limestone

cards.q: Find Château Doisy-Daëne. Commune and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Barsac; Deuxième Cru (Second Growth) in the 1855 Sauternes-Barsac classification. Part of the original Doisy estate, owned by the Dubourdieu family since 1924.
cards.hint: Barsac sits north of the Ciron on limestone

cards.q: Find Château Doisy-Dubroca. Commune and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Barsac; Deuxième Cru (Second Growth) in the 1855 Sauternes-Barsac classification. The smallest of the three Doisy estates, a few hectares of old Sémillon.
cards.hint: Barsac sits north of the Ciron on limestone

cards.q: Find Château Doisy-Védrines. Commune and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Barsac; Deuxième Cru (Second Growth) in the 1855 Sauternes-Barsac classification. The largest of the three Doisy estates and the original seat of the family, owned by the Castéja family since 1840.
cards.hint: Barsac sits north of the Ciron on limestone

cards.q: Find Château d'Arche. Commune and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Sauternes; Deuxième Cru (Second Growth) in the 1855 Sauternes-Barsac classification. A seventeenth-century château on a gravel hill in Sauternes, named after the Comte d'Arche, an eighteenth-century owner who built up the estate.
cards.hint: Sauternes commune group: Sauternes, Bommes, Fargues, Preignac

cards.q: Find Château Filhot. Commune and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Sauternes; Deuxième Cru (Second Growth) in the 1855 Sauternes-Barsac classification. A large estate in the south of Sauternes with an elegant château built in the early nineteenth century and a park.
cards.hint: Sauternes commune group: Sauternes, Bommes, Fargues, Preignac

cards.q: Find Château Broustet. Commune and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Barsac; Deuxième Cru (Second Growth) in the 1855 Sauternes-Barsac classification. A small Barsac estate on the limestone plateau beside the road to Langon, with vineyards on red sand and clay over limestone.
cards.hint: Barsac sits north of the Ciron on limestone

cards.q: Find Château Nairac. Commune and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Barsac; Deuxième Cru (Second Growth) in the 1855 Sauternes-Barsac classification. An elegant château built in 1776 for Élysée Nairac, a Protestant merchant from a family of shipowners, by an architect from the circle of Victor Louis.
cards.hint: Barsac sits north of the Ciron on limestone

cards.q: Find Château Caillou. Commune and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Barsac; Deuxième Cru (Second Growth) in the 1855 Sauternes-Barsac classification. A small estate with a neo-Gothic château on the limestone of Barsac, run by the Bravo family.
cards.hint: Barsac sits north of the Ciron on limestone

cards.q: Find Château Suau. Commune and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Barsac; Deuxième Cru (Second Growth) in the 1855 Sauternes-Barsac classification. One of the least-known classed growths, a small Barsac vineyard of a few hectares close to the Garonne.
cards.hint: Barsac sits north of the Ciron on limestone

cards.q: Find Château de Malle. Commune and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Sauternes; Deuxième Cru (Second Growth) in the 1855 Sauternes-Barsac classification. A seventeenth-century château with Italian-style gardens and statues, classified as a historic monument, in Preignac.
cards.hint: Sauternes commune group: Sauternes, Bommes, Fargues, Preignac

cards.q: Find Château Romer. Commune and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Sauternes; Deuxième Cru (Second Growth) in the 1855 Sauternes-Barsac classification. The small half of the old Romer estate in Fargues, owned by the Farges family.
cards.hint: Sauternes commune group: Sauternes, Bommes, Fargues, Preignac

cards.q: Find Château Romer du Hayot. Commune and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Sauternes; Deuxième Cru (Second Growth) in the 1855 Sauternes-Barsac classification. The other part of the old Romer estate, in Fargues, run by the du Hayot family since the 1970s.
cards.hint: Sauternes commune group: Sauternes, Bommes, Fargues, Preignac

cards.q: Find Château Lamothe. Commune and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Sauternes; Deuxième Cru (Second Growth) in the 1855 Sauternes-Barsac classification. In 1961 the old Lamothe estate on a ridge south of Sauternes village was split between two families.
cards.hint: Sauternes commune group: Sauternes, Bommes, Fargues, Preignac

cards.q: Find Château Lamothe Guignard. Commune and 1855 rank?
cards.a: Sauternes; Deuxième Cru (Second Growth) in the 1855 Sauternes-Barsac classification. The larger part of the old Lamothe estate, owned by the Guignard family since 1981, on a ridge of gravel and clay near Sauternes village.
cards.hint: Sauternes commune group: Sauternes, Bommes, Fargues, Preignac

cards.q: How many sweet wines were classified in 1855 for Sauternes and Barsac, in which tiers?
cards.a: 21 in 1855 (Yquem, 9 premiers and 11 deuxièmes crus); later divisions of estates give 27 names today: Yquem, 11 Premiers Crus and 15 Deuxièmes Crus.
cards.hint: Yquem stands alone at the top

cards.q: Which five communes may produce Sauternes, and what may Barsac wines be labelled?
cards.a: Sauternes, Bommes, Fargues, Preignac and Barsac; Barsac wines may use either Barsac or Sauternes.

decks.title: Saint-Émilion 2022: the Premiers Grands Crus
decks.description: The A and B estates of the 2022 classification and the famous withdrawals.

cards.q: Find Château Pavie. Its rank in the 2022 Saint-Émilion classification?
cards.a: Premier Grand Cru Classé A (2022), one of only two A estates (Figeac and Pavie).

cards.q: Find Château Figeac. Its rank in the 2022 Saint-Émilion classification?
cards.a: Premier Grand Cru Classé A (2022), one of only two A estates (Figeac and Pavie).

cards.q: Why is Château Ausone absent from the 2022 Saint-Émilion classification?
cards.a: It withdrew in 2021; it was formerly Premier Grand Cru Classé A. The withdrawals followed rule changes that gave weight to criteria such as wine tourism and media presence.

cards.q: Why is Château Cheval Blanc absent from the 2022 Saint-Émilion classification?
cards.a: It withdrew in 2021; it was formerly Premier Grand Cru Classé A. The withdrawals followed rule changes that gave weight to criteria such as wine tourism and media presence.

cards.q: Why is Château Angélus absent from the 2022 Saint-Émilion classification?
cards.a: It withdrew in 2022; it was formerly Premier Grand Cru Classé A. The withdrawals followed rule changes that gave weight to criteria such as wine tourism and media presence.

cards.q: Find Château Beau-Séjour Bécot. Its rank in the 2022 Saint-Émilion classification?
cards.a: Premier Grand Cru Classé B (2022).

cards.q: Find Château Beauséjour. Its rank in the 2022 Saint-Émilion classification?
cards.a: Premier Grand Cru Classé B (2022).

cards.q: Find Château Bélair-Monange. Its rank in the 2022 Saint-Émilion classification?
cards.a: Premier Grand Cru Classé B (2022).

cards.q: Find Château Canon. Its rank in the 2022 Saint-Émilion classification?
cards.a: Premier Grand Cru Classé B (2022).

cards.q: Find Château Canon-la-Gaffelière. Its rank in the 2022 Saint-Émilion classification?
cards.a: Premier Grand Cru Classé B (2022).

cards.q: Find Château Larcis Ducasse. Its rank in the 2022 Saint-Émilion classification?
cards.a: Premier Grand Cru Classé B (2022).

cards.q: Find Château Pavie Macquin. Its rank in the 2022 Saint-Émilion classification?
cards.a: Premier Grand Cru Classé B (2022).

cards.q: Find Château Troplong Mondot. Its rank in the 2022 Saint-Émilion classification?
cards.a: Premier Grand Cru Classé B (2022).

cards.q: Find Château Trotte Vieille. Its rank in the 2022 Saint-Émilion classification?
cards.a: Premier Grand Cru Classé B (2022).

cards.q: Find Château Valandraud. Its rank in the 2022 Saint-Émilion classification?
cards.a: Premier Grand Cru Classé B (2022).

cards.q: Find Clos Fourtet. Its rank in the 2022 Saint-Émilion classification?
cards.a: Premier Grand Cru Classé B (2022).

cards.q: Find La Mondotte. Its rank in the 2022 Saint-Émilion classification?
cards.a: Premier Grand Cru Classé B (2022).

cards.q: Why is Château La Gaffelière absent from the 2022 Saint-Émilion classification?
cards.a: It withdrew in 2022; it was formerly Premier Grand Cru Classé B. The withdrawals followed rule changes that gave weight to criteria such as wine tourism and media presence.

cards.q: How many estates are Premiers Grands Crus Classés in the 2022 Saint-Émilion classification?
cards.a: 14: two A (Figeac, Pavie) and 12 B. The INAO list gives 71 Grands Crus Classés below them.

cards.q: When was the first Saint-Émilion classification and how often is it revised?
cards.a: 1955; it is meant to be revised about every 10 years (1969, 1986, 1996, 2006 annulled, 2012, 2022).

cards.q: Which Saint-Émilion estates withdrew from the classification in 2021 and 2022?
cards.a: Cheval Blanc and Ausone (2021), Angélus (2022) and La Gaffelière (2022).

decks.title: Burgundy: the 33 grand crus
decks.description: Every grand cru on the map with its village and colour.

cards.q: Find Chambertin. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Gevrey-Chambertin; red (Pinot Noir). The flagship of Gevrey; Napoleon's favourite wine.

cards.q: Find Chambertin-Clos de Bèze. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Gevrey-Chambertin; red (Pinot Noir). May be sold as Chambertin; planted by the monks of Bèze in the 7th century.

cards.q: Find Chapelle-Chambertin. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Gevrey-Chambertin; red (Pinot Noir). Below Clos de Bèze; lighter, thin soils.

cards.q: Find Charmes-Chambertin. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Gevrey-Chambertin; red (Pinot Noir). Largest Gevrey grand cru; Mazoyères-Chambertin may be sold as Charmes.

cards.q: Find Mazoyères-Chambertin. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Gevrey-Chambertin; red (Pinot Noir). Usually sold as Charmes-Chambertin.

cards.q: Find Griotte-Chambertin. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Gevrey-Chambertin; red (Pinot Noir). Tiny, below Chambertin; cherry (griotte) fruit.

cards.q: Find Latricières-Chambertin. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Gevrey-Chambertin; red (Pinot Noir). Southern end, next to Chambertin, cooler air from the Combe de Grisard.

cards.q: Find Mazis-Chambertin. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Gevrey-Chambertin; red (Pinot Noir). Northern end, below Ruchottes.

cards.q: Find Ruchottes-Chambertin. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Gevrey-Chambertin; red (Pinot Noir). High, rocky, thin soil (ruchottes: rocks).

cards.q: Find Clos de la Roche. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Morey-Saint-Denis; red (Pinot Noir). Largest Morey grand cru; firm and long-lived.

cards.q: Find Clos Saint-Denis. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Morey-Saint-Denis; red (Pinot Noir). Gave its name to the village; fine, perfumed.

cards.q: Find Clos des Lambrays. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Morey-Saint-Denis; red (Pinot Noir). Promoted to grand cru in 1981; almost a monopole (LVMH).

cards.q: Find Clos de Tart. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Morey-Saint-Denis; red (Pinot Noir). Monopole since the 12th century, rows run across the slope (north to south).

cards.q: Find Bonnes-Mares. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Chambolle-Musigny and Morey-Saint-Denis; red (Pinot Noir). Straddles the two villages; terres rouges and terres blanches.

cards.q: Find Musigny. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Chambolle-Musigny; red and white. The only Côte de Nuits grand cru with red and white (Musigny Blanc, de Vogüé).

cards.q: Find Clos de Vougeot. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Vougeot; red (Pinot Noir). About 50 ha walled by the Cistercians (1110 to 1336); about 80 owners.

cards.q: Find Échezeaux. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Flagey-Échezeaux (Vosne-Romanée); red (Pinot Noir). Large and variable; lies in Flagey-Échezeaux.

cards.q: Find Grands-Échezeaux. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Flagey-Échezeaux (Vosne-Romanée); red (Pinot Noir). Smaller and more consistent, beside Clos de Vougeot.

cards.q: Find Richebourg. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Vosne-Romanée; red (Pinot Noir). Opulent, rich, above Romanée-Saint-Vivant.

cards.q: Find Romanée-Conti. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Vosne-Romanée; red (Pinot Noir). Monopole of the Domaine de la Romanée-Conti, about 1.8 ha.

cards.q: Find La Romanée. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Vosne-Romanée; red (Pinot Noir). The smallest AOC in France (0.85 ha); monopole of Liger-Belair.

cards.q: Find La Tâche. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Vosne-Romanée; red (Pinot Noir). DRC monopole, about 6 ha.

cards.q: Find Romanée-Saint-Vivant. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Vosne-Romanée; red (Pinot Noir). Below Romanée-Conti and Richebourg, named for the monks of Saint-Vivant.

cards.q: Find La Grande Rue. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Vosne-Romanée; red (Pinot Noir). Promoted 1992; monopole of Domaine François Lamarche, between La Tâche and Romanée-Conti.

cards.q: Find Corton. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Aloxe-Corton, Ladoix-Serrigny and Pernand-Vergelesses; red and white. The only red grand cru of the Côte de Beaune; many climats (Bressandes, Clos du Roi, Renardes).

cards.q: Find Corton-Charlemagne. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Aloxe-Corton, Ladoix-Serrigny and Pernand-Vergelesses; white (Chardonnay). White grand cru on the upper slopes of the Corton hill.

cards.q: Find Charlemagne. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Aloxe-Corton and Pernand-Vergelesses; white (Chardonnay). Almost never used; sold as Corton-Charlemagne.

cards.q: Find Montrachet. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Puligny-Montrachet and Chassagne-Montrachet; white (Chardonnay). Le Montrachet: about 8 ha, the summit of white Burgundy.

cards.q: Find Chevalier-Montrachet. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Puligny-Montrachet; white (Chardonnay). Above Montrachet, stonier, more mineral.

cards.q: Find Bâtard-Montrachet. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Puligny-Montrachet and Chassagne-Montrachet; white (Chardonnay). Below Montrachet, richer soils, fuller wines.

cards.q: Find Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Puligny-Montrachet; white (Chardonnay). Small enclave within Bâtard, Puligny side.

cards.q: Find Criots-Bâtard-Montrachet. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Chassagne-Montrachet; white (Chardonnay). The smallest white grand cru, about 1.6 ha.

cards.q: Find Chablis Grand Cru. Village and wine colour?
cards.a: Chablis; white (Chardonnay). One AOC of seven climats; the only grand cru outside the Côte d'Or.

cards.q: How many grand crus are there in Burgundy, and where are they?
cards.a: 33: 24 in the Côte de Nuits, 8 in the Côte de Beaune and Chablis Grand Cru (one AOC with seven climats). Each is its own AOC.

cards.q: Which Burgundy grand crus are monopoles?
cards.a: Romanée-Conti and La Tâche (DRC), La Romanée (Liger-Belair), La Grande Rue (Lamarche), Clos de Tart (Artémis); Clos des Lambrays is almost entirely one estate.

cards.q: Which grand cru is the most recent?
cards.a: La Grande Rue (1992), after Clos des Lambrays (1981).

decks.title: Côte d'Or: the village appellations
decks.description: North to south along the Côte de Nuits and Côte de Beaune.

cards.q: Find Marsannay. Which côte, and what is it known for?
cards.a: Côte de Nuits. The only Côte d'Or village AOC allowed red, white and rosé; northern gateway of the Côte de Nuits.

cards.q: Find Fixin. Which côte, and what is it known for?
cards.a: Côte de Nuits. Firm, rustic reds; Clos Napoléon and Clos de la Perrière.

cards.q: Find Gevrey-Chambertin. Which côte, and what is it known for?
cards.a: Côte de Nuits. Nine grand crus; powerful, dark, structured reds.

cards.q: Find Morey-Saint-Denis. Which côte, and what is it known for?
cards.a: Côte de Nuits. Five grand crus (including part of Bonnes-Mares); between Gevrey and Chambolle in style.

cards.q: Find Chambolle-Musigny. Which côte, and what is it known for?
cards.a: Côte de Nuits. The most perfumed, silky reds; Les Amoureuses premier cru.

cards.q: Find Vougeot. Which côte, and what is it known for?
cards.a: Côte de Nuits. Small village outside the Clos; premier cru Le Clos Blanc de Vougeot (white).

cards.q: Find Vosne-Romanée. Which côte, and what is it known for?
cards.a: Côte de Nuits. Six grand crus in the commune plus the two Échezeaux of Flagey; spicy, silky, the greatest names.

cards.q: Find Nuits-Saint-Georges. Which côte, and what is it known for?
cards.a: Côte de Nuits. No grand cru; firm, earthy reds; Les Saint-Georges premier cru; Prémeaux-Prissey in the south.

cards.q: Find Ladoix. Which côte, and what is it known for?
cards.a: Côte de Beaune. Northernmost Côte de Beaune village, part of the Corton hill.

cards.q: Find Aloxe-Corton. Which côte, and what is it known for?
cards.a: Côte de Beaune. Below the Corton hill; mostly red.

cards.q: Find Pernand-Vergelesses. Which côte, and what is it known for?
cards.a: Côte de Beaune. Western side of the Corton hill; Île des Vergelesses premier cru.

cards.q: Find Savigny-lès-Beaune. Which côte, and what is it known for?
cards.a: Côte de Beaune. Supple reds from a side valley.

cards.q: Find Chorey-lès-Beaune. Which côte, and what is it known for?
cards.a: Côte de Beaune. Flat land east of the main road; no premiers crus.

cards.q: Find Beaune. Which côte, and what is it known for?
cards.a: Côte de Beaune. The wine capital; many premiers crus (Grèves, Clos des Mouches); Hospices de Beaune auction.

cards.q: Find Pommard. Which côte, and what is it known for?
cards.a: Côte de Beaune. Sturdy, tannic reds; Rugiens and Épenots premiers crus; red only.

cards.q: Find Volnay. Which côte, and what is it known for?
cards.a: Côte de Beaune. Delicate, fragrant reds; red only; Santenots (in Meursault) sold as Volnay.

cards.q: Find Monthélie. Which côte, and what is it known for?
cards.a: Côte de Beaune. Light, fragrant reds near Volnay.

cards.q: Find Auxey-Duresses. Which côte, and what is it known for?
cards.a: Côte de Beaune. Side valley; red and white.

cards.q: Find Saint-Romain. Which côte, and what is it known for?
cards.a: Côte de Beaune. High, cool side valley behind Auxey-Duresses; mostly white.

cards.q: Find Meursault. Which côte, and what is it known for?
cards.a: Côte de Beaune. Rich, nutty whites; no grand cru; Perrières, Genevrières, Charmes premiers crus.

cards.q: Find Blagny. Which côte, and what is it known for?
cards.a: Côte de Beaune. Hamlet above Meursault and Puligny; Blagny AOC is for reds, whites sold as Meursault or Puligny premier cru.

cards.q: Find Puligny-Montrachet. Which côte, and what is it known for?
cards.a: Côte de Beaune. Taut, mineral whites; shares Montrachet and Bâtard-Montrachet.

cards.q: Find Saint-Aubin. Which côte, and what is it known for?
cards.a: Côte de Beaune. Behind Puligny and Chassagne; fine, value whites.

cards.q: Find Chassagne-Montrachet. Which côte, and what is it known for?
cards.a: Côte de Beaune. Fuller whites and some reds; shares Montrachet and Bâtard.

cards.q: Find Santenay. Which côte, and what is it known for?
cards.a: Côte de Beaune. Earthy reds, spa town.

cards.q: Find Maranges. Which côte, and what is it known for?
cards.a: Côte de Beaune. Southernmost village AOC; rustic reds.

cards.q: Find Côte de Nuits-Villages. Which communes can use it?
cards.a: Fixin, Brochon, Prissey, Comblanchien and Corgoloin; mostly red.

cards.q: What is Côte de Beaune-Villages?
cards.a: A red-only appellation that blends or labels wine from any of 16 Côte de Beaune villages (not Aloxe-Corton, Beaune, Pommard or Volnay).

decks.title: Chablis: grand cru climats and key premiers crus
decks.description: The seven climats on one slope above the Serein, plus the soil that makes them.

cards.q: Find the Chablis grand cru climat Les Clos.
cards.a: The largest and most powerful climat, about 26 ha.

cards.q: Find the Chablis grand cru climat Blanchot.
cards.a: Southeast end, cooler, floral and delicate.

cards.q: Find the Chablis grand cru climat Valmur.
cards.a: Between Les Clos and Grenouilles; rich, structured.

cards.q: Find the Chablis grand cru climat Vaudésir.
cards.a: Steep south-facing bowl; contains the unofficial La Moutonne.

cards.q: Find the Chablis grand cru climat Grenouilles.
cards.a: The smallest climat (about 9 ha), nearest the Serein; La Chablisienne's Château Grenouilles.

cards.q: Find the Chablis grand cru climat Preuses.
cards.a: High on the slope, round and elegant.

cards.q: Find the Chablis grand cru climat Bougros.
cards.a: Northwest end, steep Côte Bouguerots, sturdy wines.

cards.q: Name the seven Chablis Grand Cru climats.
cards.a: Bougros, Preuses, Vaudésir, Grenouilles, Valmur, Les Clos, Blanchot (a mnemonic: northwest to southeast along the slope).

cards.q: On which soil do Chablis Grand and Premier Crus lie?
cards.a: Kimmeridgian marl, a Jurassic limestone-clay packed with tiny Exogyra virgula oyster fossils; Petit Chablis lies on younger Portlandian limestone.

cards.q: Which unofficial grand cru vineyard lies across Vaudésir and Preuses?
cards.a: La Moutonne, a monopole of Domaine Long-Depaquit; INAO treats it as part of the grand cru.

cards.q: Find Montée de Tonnerre. Which side of the Serein, and its status?
cards.a: Right bank, next to the grand crus; one of the most prized Chablis premiers crus.

cards.q: Find Fourchaume.
cards.a: A large right-bank premier cru north of the grand crus.

cards.q: Find Vaillons.
cards.a: A left-bank premier cru, west of the town, more southeast-facing.

decks.title: Beaujolais: the ten crus
decks.description: North to south, with their granite, schist and diorite soils.

cards.q: Find the Beaujolais cru Saint-Amour.
cards.a: Northernmost cru, mixed granite and clay-limestone; soft and fruity; cru since 1946.

cards.q: Find the Beaujolais cru Juliénas.
cards.a: Firm, spicy, on schist and granite; cru since 1938.

cards.q: Find the Beaujolais cru Chénas.
cards.a: The smallest cru, sturdy; named after oak (chêne) forests.

cards.q: Find the Beaujolais cru Moulin-à-Vent.
cards.a: The most structured cru, pink granite rich in manganese; named after its windmill; no village of that name.

cards.q: Find the Beaujolais cru Fleurie.
cards.a: Pink granite, floral and silky; La Madone chapel.

cards.q: Find the Beaujolais cru Chiroubles.
cards.a: The highest cru (up to about 450 m), light and delicate.

cards.q: Find the Beaujolais cru Morgon.
cards.a: Côte du Py of blue schist and volcanic rock; firm, cherry, ages to "morgonner".

cards.q: Find the Beaujolais cru Régnié.
cards.a: The newest cru (1988), sandy granite, supple.

cards.q: Find the Beaujolais cru Brouilly.
cards.a: The largest and southernmost cru, around Mont Brouilly.

cards.q: Find the Beaujolais cru Côte de Brouilly.
cards.a: The slopes of Mont Brouilly itself, blue diorite (volcanic), more mineral.

cards.q: How many Beaujolais crus are there? Name them north to south.
cards.a: Ten: Saint-Amour, Juliénas, Chénas, Moulin-à-Vent, Fleurie, Chiroubles, Morgon, Régnié, Brouilly, Côte de Brouilly.

cards.q: Find Beaujolais-Villages. What separates it from basic Beaujolais?
cards.a: About 38 villages in the hilly granite north; the southern Pierres Dorées (limestone) area makes basic Beaujolais.

cards.q: When is Beaujolais Nouveau released?
cards.a: The third Thursday of November.

cards.q: What is semi-carbonic maceration, and how does it mark Beaujolais?
cards.a: Whole bunches in a closed vat: fermentation starts inside intact berries under CO2, giving low tannin, purple colour and banana, bubblegum and kirsch aromas.

decks.title: Rhône crus, north and south
decks.description: The 17 crus and what each is allowed to make.

cards.q: Find Côte-Rôtie. North or south, and what does it make?
cards.a: Northern Rhône. Syrah with up to 20% Viognier co-fermented; Côte Brune (schist) and Côte Blonde (granite and gneiss); steep terraces at Ampuis.

cards.q: Find Condrieu. North or south, and what does it make?
cards.a: Northern Rhône. 100% Viognier, granite terraces; dry (and rare sweet) white.

cards.q: Find Château-Grillet. North or south, and what does it make?
cards.a: Northern Rhône. Single-estate Viognier AOC (about 3.8 ha), Artémis since 2011.

cards.q: Find Saint-Joseph. North or south, and what does it make?
cards.a: Northern Rhône. Long west-bank strip; Syrah (up to 10% Marsanne or Roussanne); whites from Marsanne and Roussanne.

cards.q: Find Crozes-Hermitage. North or south, and what does it make?
cards.a: Northern Rhône. The largest northern cru; Syrah (up to 15% Marsanne or Roussanne); Les Chassis plain and northern granite hills.

cards.q: Find Hermitage. North or south, and what does it make?
cards.a: Northern Rhône. Granite hill above Tain; Syrah (up to 15% white grapes) and Marsanne-Roussanne whites; vin de paille.

cards.q: Find Cornas. North or south, and what does it make?
cards.a: Northern Rhône. 100% Syrah, granite amphitheatre, no white grapes allowed.

cards.q: Find Saint-Péray. North or south, and what does it make?
cards.a: Northern Rhône. White only (Marsanne, Roussanne), still and traditional-method sparkling.

cards.q: Find Châteauneuf-du-Pape. North or south, and what does it make?
cards.a: Southern Rhône. 13 permitted varieties (18 counting colour variants), Grenache-led; galets roulés, sand and limestone; first self-regulated AOC rules (1923).

cards.q: Find Gigondas. North or south, and what does it make?
cards.a: Southern Rhône. Below the Dentelles de Montmirail; red and rosé, Grenache min 50%.

cards.q: Find Vacqueyras. North or south, and what does it make?
cards.a: Southern Rhône. Red, white and rosé; Grenache-Syrah reds.

cards.q: Find Vinsobres. North or south, and what does it make?
cards.a: Southern Rhône. Drôme cru (2006), reds only.

cards.q: Find Rasteau. North or south, and what does it make?
cards.a: Southern Rhône. Dry red cru (2010) and Rasteau vin doux naturel.

cards.q: Find Cairanne. North or south, and what does it make?
cards.a: Southern Rhône. Cru since 2016; red and white.

cards.q: Find Beaumes-de-Venise. North or south, and what does it make?
cards.a: Southern Rhône. Dry red cru (2005); separate AOC Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise VDN.

cards.q: Find Lirac. North or south, and what does it make?
cards.a: Southern Rhône. West bank; red, white and rosé.

cards.q: Find Tavel. North or south, and what does it make?
cards.a: Southern Rhône. Rosé only, Grenache-based, deeper and fuller than Provence.

cards.q: Find Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise. North or south, and what does it make?
cards.a: Southern Rhône. Vin doux naturel from Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, min 15% abv.

cards.q: Which Rhône cru is rosé only?
cards.a: Tavel.

cards.q: Which northern Rhône red cru permits no white grapes at all?
cards.a: Cornas (100% Syrah).

cards.q: How many crus does the Rhône have? Name the eight northern ones.
cards.a: 17. North: Côte-Rôtie, Condrieu, Château-Grillet, Saint-Joseph, Crozes-Hermitage, Hermitage, Cornas, Saint-Péray.

cards.q: What are galets roulés and where are they found?
cards.a: Rounded quartzite pebbles left by the ancient Rhône; La Crau plateau of Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Lirac and Tavel; they store heat and reflect light.

decks.title: Alsace: the 51 grands crus
decks.description: Every Alsace grand cru on the map, with its soil and claim to fame.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Altenberg de Bergbieten.
cards.a: Altenberg de Bergbieten, in the northern Bas-Rhin, gives broad, spicy Riesling and Gewurztraminer from a sunny southeast slope of marl, limestone and gypsum. Soil: Marl and limestone with gypsum on a southeast-facing slope west of Strasbourg.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Altenberg de Bergheim.
cards.a: Altenberg de Bergheim is one of Alsace's historic vineyards and one of the two grands crus that may make blends of several grapes, a privilege won by Marcel Deiss, who planted it as a field blend. Soil: Jurassic limestone and marl on a south-facing slope above the walled town of Bergheim.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Altenberg de Wolxheim.
cards.a: Altenberg de Wolxheim is a limestone hill on the edge of the Bruche valley west of Strasbourg, long the city's favourite source of Riesling and reputedly a favourite of Napoleon. Soil: Limestone and marl on a southeast-facing hill west of Strasbourg.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Brand.
cards.a: Brand, meaning fire or burn, is one of the great Riesling sites of Alsace: a steep granite slope that heats up fast in the sun. Soil: Two-mica granite on a steep slope facing south and southeast above Turckheim, at the mouth of the Munster valley.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Bruderthal.
cards.a: Bruderthal, the brothers' valley, was named after the monks who farmed it. Soil: Limestone and marl with sandstone on a southeast slope above Molsheim.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Eichberg.
cards.a: Eichberg (oak hill), above the round medieval village of Eguisheim, is one of the driest and warmest sites in Alsace. Soil: Limestone and marl with sandstone scree on a southeast slope.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Engelberg.
cards.a: Engelberg, the angels' hill, straddles Dahlenheim and Scharrachbergheim at the northern end of the Route des Vins, among the northernmost grands crus. Soil: Limestone and marl at the northern end of the Route des Vins.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Florimont.
cards.a: Florimont, the hill of flowers, rises just west of Colmar between Ingersheim and Katzenthal, on limestone and marl with a sunny southern exposure. Soil: Limestone and marl on a south-facing hill west of Colmar.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Frankstein.
cards.a: Frankstein is made up of four separate granite hillsides around Dambach-la-Ville, the largest wine commune of the Bas-Rhin. Soil: Two-mica granite in four separate parcels on the slopes above Dambach-la-Ville.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Froehn.
cards.a: Froehn is a compact grand cru of about 14 ha wrapped around the hilltop village of Zellenberg, between Riquewihr and Ribeauvillé. Soil: Marl and clay with schist on a south-facing hill.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Furstentum.
cards.a: Furstentum, the principality, is a warm, sheltered amphitheatre between Kientzheim and Sigolsheim that ripens Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris to great richness, and gives powerful Riesling. Soil: Limestone with marl and sandstone on a steep south-facing slope.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Geisberg.
cards.a: Geisberg, the goat hill, is one of the smallest grands crus, about 8 ha of steep terraces above Ribeauvillé, documented since 1308. Soil: Limestone and marl with sandstone on steep terraces.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Gloeckelberg.
cards.a: Gloeckelberg, the bell hill, sits between Rodern and Saint-Hippolyte below the Haut-Koenigsbourg, on granite with sand and clay. Soil: Granite with sand and clay on a southeast slope.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Goldert.
cards.a: Goldert, golden garden, owes its name to the golden colour of its wines. Soil: Limestone and marl with sandstone on an east and southeast slope.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Hatschbourg.
cards.a: Hatschbourg spreads over a warm, sunny slope above Hattstatt and Voegtlinshoffen south of Colmar, on limestone and marl covered with loess. Soil: Limestone and marl with loess on a southeast slope.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Hengst.
cards.a: Hengst, the stallion, is one of the most powerful grands crus: its calcareous marl gives dense, spicy Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris and firm, long-lived Riesling. Soil: Limestone and marl with sandstone on a steep southeast-facing hill. One of three grands crus allowed red Pinot Noir (since 2022).

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Kaefferkopf.
cards.a: Kaefferkopf, the beetle's head, was the 51st grand cru, added in 2007 after decades of argument over its delimitation and rules. Soil: Granite, sandstone and limestone in a single 74 ha grand cru.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Kanzlerberg.
cards.a: Kanzlerberg, the chancellor's hill, is the smallest grand cru of Alsace, a little over 3 ha next to Altenberg de Bergheim. Soil: Gypsum-rich marl and limestone; the smallest grand cru at about 3 ha.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Kastelberg.
cards.a: Kastelberg, castle hill, is a steep slope of black Steiger schist above Andlau, and it is one of the great Riesling sites of the Bas-Rhin: austere, smoky and slow-ageing. Soil: Steiger schist (dark, slaty) on a steep hill above Andlau.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Kessler.
cards.a: Kessler, the cauldron, is a bowl-shaped valley on the slopes above Guebwiller, where red sandstone gives silky, spicy Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris. Soil: Pink Vosges sandstone with clay on terraced slopes in a sheltered valley.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Kirchberg de Barr.
cards.a: Kirchberg de Barr, the church hill, rises above the town of Barr and gives structured Riesling and rich Gewurztraminer. Soil: Limestone and marl on a hill above the town of Barr. One of three grands crus allowed red Pinot Noir (since 2022).

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Kirchberg de Ribeauvillé.
cards.a: Kirchberg de Ribeauvillé, the church hill, lies on a steep, sunny slope west of Ribeauvillé below the town's three ruined castles. Soil: Limestone and marl with sandstone scree on a south-facing slope.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Kitterlé.
cards.a: Kitterlé is one of the steepest grands crus, on volcanic sandstone above Guebwiller, and gives powerful, spicy Riesling and Gewurztraminer. Soil: Volcanic sandstone with spilite on a very steep terraced slope.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Mambourg.
cards.a: Mambourg is a long, warm, south-facing hill above Sigolsheim with a near-Mediterranean flora, giving rich Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris and powerful Riesling. Soil: Limestone and marl on a long south-facing hill.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Mandelberg.
cards.a: Mandelberg, almond hill, is named for the almond trees that grow in its mild microclimate between Mittelwihr and Beblenheim. Soil: Limestone and marl on a south-facing slope.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Marckrain.
cards.a: Marckrain, the boundary slope, faces east above Bennwihr and Sigolsheim, on marl and limestone that hold water and give rich, spicy Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris, often with late-harvest sweetness. Soil: Marl and limestone on an east-facing slope.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Moenchberg.
cards.a: Moenchberg, the monks' hill, lies between Andlau and Eichhoffen on a south-facing slope of marl, limestone and colluvium. Soil: Marl and limestone with colluvium on a south-facing slope.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Muenchberg.
cards.a: Muenchberg, another monks' hill, was planted by the Cistercians of Baumgarten abbey in the twelfth century. Soil: Volcanic sandstone and pebbles in a natural amphitheatre.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Ollwiller.
cards.a: Ollwiller lies below the Hartmannswillerkopf (Vieil Armand), a First World War battlefield, near the southern end of the Alsace vineyard. Soil: Sandstone and clay at the southern end of the vineyard below the Vieil Armand.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Osterberg.
cards.a: Osterberg, the eastern hill, lies next to Geisberg on the slopes north of Ribeauvillé, on marl and limestone that give more weight than its neighbour. Soil: Marl and limestone on a southeast slope.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Pfersigberg.
cards.a: Pfersigberg, the peach hill, is a large grand cru of about 71 ha above Eguisheim and Wettolsheim, on warm limestone and marl facing southeast. Soil: Limestone and marl on a long southeast slope.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Pfingstberg.
cards.a: Pfingstberg, Pentecost hill, rises above Orschwihr in the southern Haut-Rhin on a steep southeast slope of sandstone, limestone and marl. Soil: Sandstone and limestone on a steep southeast slope.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Praelatenberg.
cards.a: Praelatenberg, the prelates' hill, was owned by the monks of Ebersmunster abbey. Soil: Granite and gneiss below the castle of Haut-Koenigsbourg.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Rangen.
cards.a: Rangen is the southernmost grand cru and one of the most extraordinary vineyards in France: a very steep, south-facing wall of volcanic rock above the Thur river at Thann. Soil: Volcanic rock (andesite, tuffs and greywacke) on an extremely steep south-facing slope.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Rosacker.
cards.a: Rosacker, the field of roses, above Hunawihr and its fortified church, gives taut, mineral, long-lived Riesling. Soil: Dolomitic limestone and marl on an east-facing slope.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Saering.
cards.a: Saering is the most northerly of Guebwiller's four grands crus, on terraced slopes of limestone, marl and sandstone facing east and southeast. Soil: Limestone and marl with sandstone on terraced slopes.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Schlossberg.
cards.a: Schlossberg, castle hill, was the first Alsace grand cru, created by decree in 1975. Soil: Granite with sand on steep terraces.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Schoenenbourg.
cards.a: Schoenenbourg, the beautiful castle, rises behind the medieval walls of Riquewihr and was famous across Europe in the sixteenth century. Soil: Keuper marl with gypsum, sandstone and dolomite on a north and northeast-facing amphitheatre above Riquewihr.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Sommerberg.
cards.a: Sommerberg, summer hill, is a steep granite slope above Niedermorschwihr that gives some of the most precise, mineral Rieslings in Alsace, notably from Albert Boxler. Soil: Granite on extremely steep terraces.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Sonnenglanz.
cards.a: Sonnenglanz, sunshine glow, is a warm, sheltered slope above Beblenheim known for rich Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris and for botrytised sweet wines. Soil: Limestone and marl on a gentle southeast slope.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Spiegel.
cards.a: Spiegel, the mirror, lies between Bergholtz and Guebwiller on sandstone and marl facing east and southeast. Soil: Sandstone and marl on a southeast slope.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Sporen.
cards.a: Sporen, next to Schoenenbourg, is traditionally planted with Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris and was once used for a famous field blend (Gentil). Soil: Clay and marl with stones on a gentle slope east of Riquewihr.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Steinert.
cards.a: Steinert, the stony one, is a hot, steep limestone slope above Pfaffenheim and Westhalten, so stony that the soil warms quickly in spring. Soil: Limestone on a steep, stony slope.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Steingrubler.
cards.a: Steingrubler, the stone quarry, lies above Wettolsheim on a mixed soil of limestone, sandstone and granite, a reflection of the faulting that shattered the Vosges foothills here. Soil: Limestone, sandstone and granite in a mixed soil.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Steinklotz.
cards.a: Steinklotz, block of stone, is the northernmost grand cru, above Marlenheim, where the Merovingian kings had a royal estate. Soil: Limestone with marl at the northern gateway of the Route des Vins.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Vorbourg.
cards.a: Vorbourg is a large, warm grand cru between Rouffach and Westhalten. Soil: Limestone and sandstone on a sunny, south-facing hill. One of three grands crus allowed red Pinot Noir (since 2022).

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Wiebelsberg.
cards.a: Wiebelsberg rises above Andlau on light, quartz-rich sandstone facing southeast, in contrast to neighbouring Kastelberg's black schist. Soil: Quartz-rich sandstone on a southeast slope above Andlau.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Wineck-Schlossberg.
cards.a: Wineck-Schlossberg lies below the ruined tower of the Wineck castle at Katzenthal and Ammerschwihr, on a steep granite slope in a side valley west of Colmar. Soil: Granite below the ruined castle of Wineck.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Winzenberg.
cards.a: Winzenberg, the winegrowers' hill, rises above Blienschwiller in the Bas-Rhin on two-mica granite facing south. Soil: Granite on a south-facing slope.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Zinnkoepflé.
cards.a: Zinnkoepflé is one of the highest and driest grands crus, a steep south-facing hill above the Vallée Noble where wild orchids and Mediterranean plants grow. Soil: Limestone and sandstone on a high, hot, south-facing slope up to about 420 m.

cards.q: Find the Alsace grand cru Zotzenberg.
cards.a: Zotzenberg, above Mittelbergheim, is the only grand cru allowed to make Sylvaner (since 2006), a tribute to a local grape long prized here. Soil: Limestone and marl on a southeast slope above Mittelbergheim.

cards.q: How many Alsace grands crus are there, and which grapes are normally permitted?
cards.a: 51 (each its own AOC since 2011). Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat; Sylvaner in Zotzenberg; blends in Altenberg de Bergheim and Kaefferkopf; Pinot Noir in Hengst, Kirchberg de Barr and Vorbourg since 2022.

cards.q: Which was the first Alsace grand cru, and when?
cards.a: Schlossberg (Kientzheim), by decree in 1975; 25 sites were named in 1983 and the list reached 50 in 1992; Kaefferkopf became the 51st in 2007.

cards.q: What do VT and SGN mean on an Alsace label?
cards.a: Vendanges Tardives (late harvest, often passerillé) and Sélection de Grains Nobles (botrytis); only from the four noble grapes.

cards.q: Name the Alsace grands crus on granite.
cards.a: Brand, Schlossberg, Sommerberg, Frankstein, Winzenberg, Wineck-Schlossberg and Gloeckelberg; Praelatenberg is granite and gneiss. Granite gives taut, aromatic, early-ripening Riesling.

cards.q: Which Alsace grands crus are volcanic?
cards.a: Rangen (andesite and tuffs at Thann), plus the volcanic sandstone of Kitterlé and Muenchberg.

decks.title: Champagne: grand cru villages and sub-regions
decks.description: The 17 grand crus, key premiers crus, the five sub-regions and label law.

cards.q: Find the Champagne grand cru village Ambonnay. Sub-region and main grape?
cards.a: Montagne de Reims; mostly Pinot Noir. Krug's Clos d'Ambonnay.

cards.q: Find the Champagne grand cru village Avize. Sub-region and main grape?
cards.a: Côte des Blancs; mostly Chardonnay. Home of Jacques Selosse.

cards.q: Find the Champagne grand cru village Aÿ. Sub-region and main grape?
cards.a: Vallée de la Marne (Grande Vallée); mostly Pinot Noir. Historic Pinot Noir village; Bollinger.

cards.q: Find the Champagne grand cru village Beaumont-sur-Vesle. Sub-region and main grape?
cards.a: Montagne de Reims; mostly Pinot Noir.

cards.q: Find the Champagne grand cru village Bouzy. Sub-region and main grape?
cards.a: Montagne de Reims; mostly Pinot Noir. Also known for Bouzy Rouge (Coteaux Champenois).

cards.q: Find the Champagne grand cru village Chouilly. Sub-region and main grape?
cards.a: Côte des Blancs; mostly Chardonnay. Promoted to grand cru in 1985.

cards.q: Find the Champagne grand cru village Cramant. Sub-region and main grape?
cards.a: Côte des Blancs; mostly Chardonnay. Chalky Chardonnay heart of the Côte des Blancs.

cards.q: Find the Champagne grand cru village Louvois. Sub-region and main grape?
cards.a: Montagne de Reims; mostly Pinot Noir.

cards.q: Find the Champagne grand cru village Mailly-Champagne. Sub-region and main grape?
cards.a: Montagne de Reims; mostly Pinot Noir.

cards.q: Find the Champagne grand cru village Le Mesnil-sur-Oger. Sub-region and main grape?
cards.a: Côte des Blancs; mostly Chardonnay. Promoted in 1985; Krug Clos du Mesnil and Salon.

cards.q: Find the Champagne grand cru village Oger. Sub-region and main grape?
cards.a: Côte des Blancs; mostly Chardonnay. Promoted in 1985.

cards.q: Find the Champagne grand cru village Oiry. Sub-region and main grape?
cards.a: Côte des Blancs; mostly Chardonnay. Promoted in 1985.

cards.q: Find the Champagne grand cru village Puisieulx. Sub-region and main grape?
cards.a: Montagne de Reims; mostly Pinot Noir.

cards.q: Find the Champagne grand cru village Sillery. Sub-region and main grape?
cards.a: Montagne de Reims; mostly Pinot Noir.

cards.q: Find the Champagne grand cru village Tours-sur-Marne. Sub-region and main grape?
cards.a: Montagne de Reims (Marne side); mostly Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Historically rated 100% for black grapes but lower for white grapes.

cards.q: Find the Champagne grand cru village Verzenay. Sub-region and main grape?
cards.a: Montagne de Reims; mostly Pinot Noir. North-facing Pinot Noir; the Verzenay lighthouse.

cards.q: Find the Champagne grand cru village Verzy. Sub-region and main grape?
cards.a: Montagne de Reims; mostly Pinot Noir. Promoted in 1985; the twisted Faux de Verzy beeches.

cards.q: Find the premier cru village Hautvillers.
cards.a: Premier Cru village; UNESCO World Heritage (2015).

cards.q: Find the premier cru village Mareuil-sur-Aÿ.
cards.a: Premier Cru village; UNESCO World Heritage (2015).

cards.q: Find the premier cru village Cumières.
cards.a: Premier Cru village.

cards.q: Find the premier cru village Dizy.
cards.a: Premier Cru village.

cards.q: Find the premier cru village Vertus.
cards.a: Premier Cru village.

cards.q: Find the premier cru village Chigny-les-Roses.
cards.a: Premier Cru village.

cards.q: Find the premier cru village Rilly-la-Montagne.
cards.a: Premier Cru village.

cards.q: Find the premier cru village Avenay-Val-d'Or.
cards.a: Premier Cru village.

cards.q: Find the premier cru village Trépail.
cards.a: Premier Cru village.

cards.q: Find the premier cru village Cuis.
cards.a: Premier Cru village.

cards.q: Find the premier cru village Villers-Marmery.
cards.a: Premier Cru village.

cards.q: Find the premier cru village Bisseuil.
cards.a: Premier Cru village.

cards.q: Find the Montagne de Reims. Main grape and character?
cards.a: Pinot Noir on chalk; structure and red fruit; ten of the 17 grand crus.

cards.q: Find the Côte des Blancs. Main grape?
cards.a: Chardonnay on pure belemnite chalk; finesse and acidity for blanc de blancs.

cards.q: Find the Vallée de la Marne. Main grape?
cards.a: Meunier (frost-hardy in the valley), with Pinot Noir in the Grande Vallée around Aÿ.

cards.q: Find the Côte des Bar (Aube). Soil and grape?
cards.a: Kimmeridgian marl like Chablis, closer to Burgundy than to Reims; mostly Pinot Noir; also Rosé des Riceys.

cards.q: Find the Côte de Sézanne.
cards.a: South of the Côte des Blancs, Chardonnay on chalk and clay; riper style.

cards.q: How many grand and premier cru villages does Champagne have?
cards.a: 17 grand crus and 42 premiers crus (Tom Stevenson, GuildSomm). Five villages were promoted to grand cru in 1985: Chouilly, Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, Oger, Oiry and Verzy.

cards.q: What was the échelle des crus and when did it end?
cards.a: A percentage scale (80 to 100%) rating each village for grape prices; grand crus were 100%, premiers 90 to 99%. Fixed grape prices ended in 1990; the échelle itself was abolished in 2010.

cards.q: Minimum lees ageing for non-vintage and vintage Champagne?
cards.a: Non-vintage: 15 months from tirage (12 on lees). Vintage: 3 years from tirage.

cards.q: What do NM, RM, CM and RC mean on a Champagne label?
cards.a: Négociant-manipulant (house buying grapes), récoltant-manipulant (grower producing from own grapes), coopérative de manipulation, récoltant-coopérateur.

cards.q: Order the dosage terms from driest to sweetest.
cards.a: Brut Nature (0 to 3 g/l, no added sugar), Extra Brut (0 to 6), Brut (under 12), Extra Dry (12 to 17), Sec (17 to 32), Demi-Sec (32 to 50), Doux (over 50).

cards.q: What is Coteaux Champenois?
cards.a: The still-wine AOC of the Champagne zone, red, white or rosé (Bouzy Rouge is the best known).

cards.q: What is Rosé des Riceys?
cards.a: A rare still rosé of Pinot Noir from Les Riceys in the Aube, one of three AOCs in that commune.

decks.title: Loire: key appellations
decks.description: From Muscadet to Sancerre: grape and style for the exam-relevant AOCs.

cards.q: Find Muscadet Sèvre et Maine. Sub-region and wine?
cards.a: Pays Nantais. Melon de Bourgogne; sur lie; crus communaux such as Clisson, Gorges and Le Pallet with long lees ageing.

cards.q: Find Gros Plant du Pays Nantais. Sub-region and wine?
cards.a: Pays Nantais. Folle Blanche: tart, light white for oysters.

cards.q: Find Savennières. Sub-region and wine?
cards.a: Anjou. Dry Chenin on schist and volcanic rock; austere, long-lived.

cards.q: Find Savennières Roche aux Moines. Sub-region and wine?
cards.a: Anjou. Savennières sub-appellation on steep schist.

cards.q: Find Coulée de Serrant. Sub-region and wine?
cards.a: Anjou. Monopole AOC of Nicolas Joly, biodynamic since the 1980s.

cards.q: Find Coteaux du Layon. Sub-region and wine?
cards.a: Anjou. Sweet Chenin from botrytis and passerillage along the Layon.

cards.q: Find Bonnezeaux. Sub-region and wine?
cards.a: Anjou. Sweet Chenin cru on schist slopes of the Layon.

cards.q: Find Quarts de Chaume. Sub-region and wine?
cards.a: Anjou. Sweet Chenin; the only Loire Grand Cru AOC (2011).

cards.q: Find Coteaux de l'Aubance. Sub-region and wine?
cards.a: Anjou. Lighter sweet Chenin.

cards.q: Find Rosé d'Anjou. Sub-region and wine?
cards.a: Anjou. Off-dry rosé, mainly Grolleau.

cards.q: Find Cabernet d'Anjou. Sub-region and wine?
cards.a: Anjou. Off-dry rosé from Cabernet Franc and Cabernet Sauvignon.

cards.q: Find Saumur. Sub-region and wine?
cards.a: Saumur. Chenin whites on tuffeau, reds, and traditional-method Saumur mousseux.

cards.q: Find Saumur-Champigny. Sub-region and wine?
cards.a: Saumur. Supple, fruity Cabernet Franc on tuffeau.

cards.q: Find Chinon. Sub-region and wine?
cards.a: Touraine. Cabernet Franc on gravel, sand and tuffeau; also rosé and Chenin white.

cards.q: Find Bourgueil. Sub-region and wine?
cards.a: Touraine. Firmer Cabernet Franc north of the Loire.

cards.q: Find Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil. Sub-region and wine?
cards.a: Touraine. Lighter, sandier Cabernet Franc next to Bourgueil.

cards.q: Find Vouvray. Sub-region and wine?
cards.a: Touraine. Chenin on tuffeau and silex clay; sec to moelleux and sparkling.

cards.q: Find Montlouis-sur-Loire. Sub-region and wine?
cards.a: Touraine. Chenin opposite Vouvray, south bank; still and Montlouis pétillant naturel.

cards.q: Find Touraine. Sub-region and wine?
cards.a: Touraine. Regional AOC: Sauvignon Blanc whites, Gamay and Côt reds.

cards.q: Find Cheverny. Sub-region and wine?
cards.a: Touraine. Sauvignon Blanc blended with Chardonnay or Menu Pineau; reds from Pinot Noir and Gamay.

cards.q: Find Cour-Cheverny. Sub-region and wine?
cards.a: Touraine. Romorantin only.

cards.q: Find Jasnières. Sub-region and wine?
cards.a: Touraine. Chenin on the Loir, a tributary; steely, dry.

cards.q: Find Sancerre. Sub-region and wine?
cards.a: Centre-Loire. Sauvignon Blanc (Kimmeridgian marl, caillottes, silex); reds and rosés from Pinot Noir.

cards.q: Find Pouilly-Fumé. Sub-region and wine?
cards.a: Centre-Loire. Sauvignon Blanc on silex and Kimmeridgian marl, across the river from Sancerre.

cards.q: Find Pouilly-sur-Loire. Sub-region and wine?
cards.a: Centre-Loire. Chasselas, a historic table-grape specialty.

cards.q: Find Menetou-Salon. Sub-region and wine?
cards.a: Centre-Loire. Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir, southwest of Sancerre.

cards.q: Find Quincy. Sub-region and wine?
cards.a: Centre-Loire. Sauvignon Blanc on sand and gravel by the Cher.

cards.q: Find Reuilly. Sub-region and wine?
cards.a: Centre-Loire. Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir and Pinot Gris (rosé).

cards.q: Find Crémant de Loire. Sub-region and wine?
cards.a: Loire. Traditional-method sparkling across Anjou, Saumur and Touraine.

cards.q: Which Loire AOC is the only Grand Cru?
cards.a: Quarts de Chaume (2011), sweet Chenin Blanc.

cards.q: Name the Muscadet crus communaux recognised in 2011.
cards.a: Clisson, Gorges and Le Pallet; others followed, including Château-Thébaud, Monnières-Saint-Fiacre and Mouzillon-Tillières, with more proposed.

cards.q: What is tuffeau and where does it matter?
cards.a: A soft, porous Turonian limestone of the middle Loire (Vouvray, Saumur, Chinon); it holds water and is carved into cellars.

decks.title: Italy: every DOCG by region
decks.description: All DOCGs on the map, sorted by region, with grapes and dates.

cards.q: Find Casauria. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Abruzzo. Montepulciano minimum 90%. Subzone 2006; DOCG 2025.

cards.q: Find Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Colline Teramane. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Abruzzo. Montepulciano minimum 90%. Subzone 1995; DOCG 2003; renamed 2016.

cards.q: Find Terre Tollesi. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Abruzzo. Montepulciano; Pecorino, Passerina, Trebbiano. DOC 2008; DOCG 2019.

cards.q: Find Aglianico del Vulture Superiore. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Basilicata. 100% Aglianico. DOCG 2010.

cards.q: Find Cirò Classico. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Calabria. Gaglioppo minimum 90%, Magliocco and/or Greco Nero up to 10%. DOCG 2025 (EU registration 18 July 2025).

cards.q: Find Aglianico del Taburno. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Campania. Aglianico minimum 85%. DOC 1986; DOCG 2011.

cards.q: Find Fiano di Avellino. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Campania. Fiano minimum 85%. DOC 1978; DOCG 2003.

cards.q: Find Greco di Tufo. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Campania. Greco minimum 85%, Coda di Volpe up to 15%. DOC 1970; DOCG 2003.

cards.q: Find Taurasi. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Campania. Aglianico minimum 85%. DOC 1970; DOCG 1993 (first in southern Italy).

cards.q: Find Colli Bolognesi Classico Pignoletto. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Emilia-Romagna. Grechetto Gentile (Pignoletto) min 85%. DOCG 2011.

cards.q: Find Romagna Albana. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Emilia-Romagna. Albana (min 95%). DOC 1967, DOCG 1987.

cards.q: Find Colli Orientali del Friuli Picolit. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Friuli Venezia Giulia. Picolit (min 85%). DOCG 2006.

cards.q: Find Ramandolo. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Friuli Venezia Giulia. Verduzzo Friulano (Verduzzo Giallo) 100%. DOCG 2001.

cards.q: Find Rosazzo. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Friuli Venezia Giulia. Friulano (min 50%), Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Pinot Bianco, Ribolla Gialla. DOCG 2011.

cards.q: Find Cannellino di Frascati. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Lazio. Malvasia minimum 70%. DOCG 2011.

cards.q: Find Cesanese del Piglio. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Lazio. Cesanese (di Affile and/or Comune) minimum 90%. DOC 1973; DOCG 2008.

cards.q: Find Frascati Superiore. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Lazio. Malvasia minimum 70%. DOCG 2011.

cards.q: Find Franciacorta. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Lombardy. Chardonnay, Pinot Nero, Pinot Bianco (max 50%), Erbamat (max 10%). DOC 1967, DOCG 1995.

cards.q: Find Oltrepò Pavese metodo classico. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Lombardy. Pinot Nero (min 70%), Chardonnay, Pinot Bianco, Pinot Grigio. DOCG 2007.

cards.q: Find Scanzo. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Lombardy. Moscato di Scanzo (100%). DOC 2002, DOCG 2009.

cards.q: Find Sforzato di Valtellina. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Lombardy. Nebbiolo (Chiavennasca) min 90%. DOCG 2003.

cards.q: Find Valtellina Superiore. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Lombardy. Nebbiolo (Chiavennasca) min 90%. DOC 1968, DOCG 1998.

cards.q: Find Castelli di Jesi Verdicchio Riserva. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Marche. Verdicchio minimum 85%. DOCG 2010 (renamed 2011).

cards.q: Find Cònero. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Marche. Montepulciano minimum 85%, Sangiovese up to 15%. Rosso Cònero DOC 1967; Cònero (Riserva) DOCG 2004.

cards.q: Find Offida. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Marche. Pecorino or Passerina (minimum 85% each); Rosso from Montepulciano minimum 85%. DOC 2001; DOCG 2011.

cards.q: Find Verdicchio di Matelica Riserva. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Marche. Verdicchio minimum 85%. DOCG 2010.

cards.q: Find Vernaccia di Serrapetrona. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Marche. Vernaccia Nera minimum 85%. DOC 1971; DOCG 2004.

cards.q: Find Alta Langa. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Piedmont. Pinot Nero and Chardonnay (min 90% together). DOC 2002, DOCG 2011.

cards.q: Find Asti. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Piedmont. Moscato Bianco (100%). DOC 1967, DOCG 1993.

cards.q: Find Barbaresco. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Piedmont. Nebbiolo (100%). DOC 1966, DOCG 1980.

cards.q: Find Barbera d'Asti. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Piedmont. Barbera (min 90%). DOC 1970, DOCG 2008.

cards.q: Find Barbera del Monferrato Superiore. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Piedmont. Barbera (min 85%). DOCG 2008.

cards.q: Find Barolo. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Piedmont. Nebbiolo (100%). DOC 1966, DOCG 1980.

cards.q: Find Brachetto d'Acqui. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Piedmont. Brachetto (min 97%). DOC 1969, DOCG 1996.

cards.q: Find Canelli. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Piedmont. Moscato Bianco (100%). DOCG 2023.

cards.q: Find Dogliani. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Piedmont. Dolcetto (100%). DOCG 2005 (Superiore), 2011 single DOCG.

cards.q: Find Dolcetto di Diano d'Alba. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Piedmont. Dolcetto (100%). DOC 1974, DOCG 2010.

cards.q: Find Dolcetto di Ovada Superiore. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Piedmont. Dolcetto (100%). DOCG 2008.

cards.q: Find Erbaluce di Caluso. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Piedmont. Erbaluce (100%). DOC 1967, DOCG 2010.

cards.q: Find Gattinara. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Piedmont. Nebbiolo (Spanna) min 90%, Vespolina and Uva Rara up to 10%. DOC 1967, DOCG 1990.

cards.q: Find Gavi. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Piedmont. Cortese (100%). DOC 1974, DOCG 1998.

cards.q: Find Ghemme. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Piedmont. Nebbiolo (min 85%), Vespolina and Uva Rara. DOC 1969, DOCG 1997.

cards.q: Find Nizza. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Piedmont. Barbera (100%). Subzone 2000, DOCG 2014 (separately registered 2019).

cards.q: Find Roero. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Piedmont. Nebbiolo (min 95%) for Roero; Arneis (min 95%) for Roero Arneis. DOC 1985, DOCG 2004.

cards.q: Find Ruchè di Castagnole Monferrato. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Piedmont. Ruchè (min 90%). DOC 1987, DOCG 2010.

cards.q: Find Terre Alfieri. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Piedmont. Arneis (min 85%) or Nebbiolo (min 85%). DOC 2009, DOCG 2020.

cards.q: Find Castel del Monte Bombino Nero. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Puglia. Bombino Nero minimum 90%. DOCG 2011.

cards.q: Find Castel del Monte Nero di Troia Riserva. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Puglia. Nero di Troia minimum 90%. DOCG 2011.

cards.q: Find Castel del Monte Rosso Riserva. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Puglia. Nero di Troia minimum 65%, with Aglianico, Montepulciano and others. DOCG 2011.

cards.q: Find Primitivo di Manduria Dolce Naturale. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Puglia. 100% Primitivo. DOCG 2011.

cards.q: Find Vermentino di Gallura. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Sardinia. Vermentino minimum 95%. DOC 1975; DOCG 1996 (Sardinia's only DOCG).

cards.q: Find Cerasuolo di Vittoria. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Sicily. Nero d'Avola 50 to 70%, Frappato 30 to 50%. DOC 1973; DOCG 2005 (Sicily's only DOCG).

cards.q: Find Brunello di Montalcino. Region, grapes and status history?
cards.a: Tuscany. 100% Sangiovese (locally Brunello). DOC 1966; DOCG 1980 (one of the first four).

cards.q: Find Carmignano. Region, grapes and status history?
